question: A colleague built and applied a Terraform configuration from their laptop. You clone the repo, use the same AWS account and profile, run terraform init and then terraform plan — and the plan proposes to create every resource in the config, even though they all already exist and are serving traffic. What explains this, and what is the structural fix?
choices: The state file — Terraform's mapping between config and real resources — was rightly never committed and lives only on the colleague's laptop; without it Terraform cannot distinguish "doesn't exist yet" from "exists and is managed by me". The fix is a remote backend (e.g. S3), which shares state and adds locking against concurrent applies
terraform init re-downloaded newer provider plugins, and that version drift makes existing resources unrecognizable to the planner; pinning versions in required_providers reconciles the plan
terraform plan works offline against the configuration alone and never queries the live API — only apply contacts AWS, so only apply would discover the existing resources
Terraform matches infrastructure to configuration by resource local name, and the colleague used different block names; renaming the resource blocks to match would reconcile the plan
explanation: plan compares three things: the config (desired), the state (what Terraform last knew), and reality — but it refreshes reality only for resources recorded in state. With no state file present, nothing is tracked, so every resource looks like it needs creating; applying would attempt duplicates or collide on names. The state file is also the reason the fix is a backend rather than git: state can contain secrets in plaintext, so committing it is wrong — a remote backend gives shared source-of-truth state, access control, and locking so two applies cannot corrupt it concurrently. The distractors misplace the mechanism: provider version drift doesn't orphan resources (tracking lives in state, not in the plugin), plan absolutely does query the live API for refresh — just only for what state lists — and matching is by the IDs recorded in state, not by config block names.

question: A reusable module makes its S3 bucket optional with count = var.bucket_name != "" ? 1 : 0. Its outputs.tf exposes value = aws_s3_bucket.this.arn, and now even callers that DO pass a bucket name fail: 'Because aws_s3_bucket.this has count set, its attributes must be accessed on specific instances.' A teammate proposes deleting the count so the module always creates the bucket. What is the mental model to fix, and the sanctioned pattern?
choices: The output is evaluated before the resource exists in the graph; a bare reference isn't enough for optional resources, so the output needs an explicit depends_on pointing at the bucket
Conditional resources fight the declarative model — the clean design is two modules, with-bucket and without-bucket, and each caller picks one; a module whose contents vary by input is the real smell

count changes the resource's type, not just its quantity: the moment a resource carries count it becomes a list — even at count = 1 — so every reference must select an instance: aws_s3_bucket.this[0].arn. And because that list can be empty, any expression that might evaluate when the bucket doesn't exist needs its own guard: local.create_bucket ? aws_s3_bucket.this[0].arn : "". That shared condition is exactly why it earns a named local — one rule read by the resource, the output, and any sibling resources it gates. Deleting count removes the error by deleting the feature: callers that want no bucket get one anyway. The modern refinement is for_each, whose named instances (this["main"]) avoid positional indexing entirely

The ternary belongs on the argument, not the resource: bucket = var.bucket_name == "" ? null : var.bucket_name tells Terraform not to create the bucket when no name is supplied, keeping the resource address a plain single object
explanation: The error is a type error, not an ordering problem: count re-types the resource from 'one object' to 'a list of objects', and Terraform enforces the new shape everywhere — including references written before count was added, which is why callers who do get a bucket still fail. The complete pattern therefore has two halves: index every reference (this[0]) and guard every reference that can run against the empty list, returning a sentinel like "" so downstream code stays evaluable in both worlds. Naming the condition as a local (create_bucket) is what keeps those halves consistent as the condition spreads to the bucket's versioning, encryption, and policy resources — one line to change, not five. The distractors trade the feature away or misdiagnose: depends_on addresses ordering, but references already create implicit dependencies and the plan never got that far — it failed at addressing; duplicating the module resolves a one-line ternary by forking an entire maintenance surface, when local + count is the documented idiom for one-or-none; and a null argument is not an off switch — Terraform treats it as 'argument unset', which for a required argument is a validation error, never 'skip this resource'. count and for_each are the only cardinality levers a resource has, and for_each's stable keys are the upgrade path when positional [0] starts to churn.

question: A new service's Terraform configuration must create a security group inside the company's existing production VPC, which is created and managed by the platform team's separate configuration. Wanting something to reference for vpc_id, a developer writes resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" } mirroring the real VPC — and terraform plan proposes '+ aws_vpc.main will be created'. What concept was misapplied, and what is the right primitive?
choices: The missing step is terraform import: the resource block is correct, but Terraform's state doesn't yet know the VPC exists — importing it maps the block to the real resource, after which plan shows no changes

The reference should be an input variable: declare variable "vpc_id" and supply the real ID through per-environment tfvars files — variables exist precisely so values that differ per environment stay out of the source

The sanctioned channel is the platform team's remote state: they add an output for the VPC ID, and consumers read it via a terraform_remote_state data source — the only correct way for one configuration to reference another's resources

A resource block is a claim of ownership — 'this configuration manages this object's lifecycle' — so Terraform, finding no matching VPC in its own state, plans to create a second one; with an import it would go further and become able to modify or destroy infrastructure another team owns. Reading something that exists but belongs elsewhere is exactly what a data source is for: data "aws_vpc" with a tag filter fetches it read-only, the reference data.aws_vpc.main.id both supplies the value and gives Terraform the dependency ordering, and the configuration stays portable — no hard-coded ID to go stale when the VPC is ever recreated, and the ownership boundary survives: only the platform team's configuration can change or destroy the VPC
explanation: The misapplied concept is what a resource block means. It is not 'a thing I want to talk about' — it is a declaration of desired state that this configuration is responsible for realizing and maintaining. Terraform compares that declaration against its own state file, and since this config never created a VPC, the honest plan is to create one: the tool is working correctly on a wrong premise. The read/write split is the design lesson: resources create and manage; data sources fetch what already exists, read-only, at plan time. A data source with a tag filter gives everything the developer actually wanted — a value to reference, an implicit dependency so ordering is right, and insulation from hard-coded IDs — while leaving the VPC's lifecycle untouched. The distractors are graded traps. Import is the most dangerous: it 'fixes' the plan output by making this configuration a second manager of the platform team's VPC — from then on, a drifted attribute in this repo's block shows up as a proposed modification, and a terraform destroy here would take the production VPC with it; import is for adopting resources you own, not for referencing resources you don't. The variable approach mechanically works but demotes a fact Terraform can query into manual bookkeeping: the ID must be discovered by a human, copied per environment, and silently goes stale if the VPC is recreated — variables are the module's knobs for caller decisions, not a channel for facts about existing reality. Remote state is a legitimate pattern (it is how configurations share computed values), but it is not 'the only correct way' — it couples you to the other team's backend access and output discipline, when a provider data source reads the same fact directly from the API with no cross-team contract needed.

question: One file holds resource "aws_s3_bucket" "artifacts" { bucket = "acme-ml-artifacts" } and, below it, an aws_s3_bucket_versioning resource whose argument was written as bucket = "acme-ml-artifacts" — the literal name repeated instead of aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id. terraform validate passes, and the first apply into an empty account fails roughly half the time with NoSuchBucket; re-running apply then succeeds. What is the underlying design mistake?
choices: HCL is evaluated top-to-bottom, so the ordering here is accidental rather than guaranteed; the durable fix is to stop relying on within-file position and split creation and configuration into two configurations applied in sequence

The value was supplied without creating a dependency. A reference like aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id does two jobs at once — it yields the value and declares an edge in the dependency graph — and Terraform provisions independent nodes of that graph in parallel. A matching string is not a reference, so no edge exists, the versioning resource can be attempted concurrently with the bucket, and the intermittency is the signature of that race rather than of a flaky API. Restoring the reference fixes ordering and the duplication in one move: the bucket name is now stated once, and it keeps working when the literal becomes var.bucket_name

Newly created S3 buckets are not immediately visible to subsequent API calls, so no ordering mechanism can help; the correct fix is to absorb the propagation delay with a wait — a time_sleep resource between the two, or the provider's retry configuration

Implicit dependencies are inferred only from attributes that are unknown until apply, so a statically-known bucket name can never produce an edge; ordering between two such resources therefore has to be stated with an explicit depends_on, which is why depends_on is standard practice on every related pair
explanation: Terraform's execution order is not the file's order and not the author's intent — it is the graph it derives from references. Every reference to another resource's address becomes an edge; everything with no path between it and another node is fair game to run concurrently, which is exactly why a missing edge shows up as a coin-flip failure instead of a deterministic one. Reading the symptom that way is the transferable skill: intermittent 'not found' during a first apply means a dependency that exists in reality was never expressed in code. The fix is also the DRY fix — a repeated literal is a fact duplicated in two places that must be edited twice and silently decays the moment the name becomes a variable, while a reference cannot go stale. The distractors each substitute a weaker mechanism for the missing edge. File order is irrelevant in a declarative configuration, and splitting into two applied configurations fragments state and adds a manual sequencing step to express what one reference expresses for free. The wait is the most tempting: it appears to work because it changes the timing of the race, but it encodes a guess about latency rather than a dependency, still runs the two nodes concurrently, and leaves the plan free to reorder them — a retry or sleep is for genuine eventual consistency after ordering is already correct, and here re-running apply succeeds simply because the bucket now exists. The last option inverts the rule: an implicit dependency comes from the reference itself, whether or not the value is computed, and reaching for depends_on on every pair replaces an automatically-derived graph with a hand-maintained one that drifts as the config grows. depends_on is reserved for real dependencies that carry no data between the resources.

question: Three sibling directories — envs/dev, envs/staging, envs/prod — each hold the same 40 lines describing a Redis cluster, differing only in node_type and vpc_id. A fix to the parameter group had to be pasted three times and prod was missed. A developer proposes collapsing all three into a single configuration that creates every environment's resources at once, with count over a list of environments. What is the sound design, and what must stay at the root?
choices: Collapse as proposed — one configuration with count over the environment list removes the duplication at its source, keeps the per-environment values visible together in that list, and makes a single apply keep all three environments in step by construction

Keep the three directories and share the common blocks as one file each environment includes, since Terraform reads every .tf in a directory as a single configuration — sharing the text is the minimal fix and avoids inventing a module interface

Use workspaces: one directory and one configuration with a workspace per environment, which is Terraform's supported answer to per-environment infrastructure — separate state per workspace, single copy of the code, and terraform.workspace to switch the values that differ

Extract the 40 lines into a child module whose variable blocks are exactly the values that differ (node_type, vpc_id) and whose output blocks expose what callers need (endpoint, security-group id); each environment root then shrinks to a module block plus its own provider and backend configuration. The split of responsibilities is the point: the child module is a component and must not pin a region, an account, or a state location, while the root module owns provider configuration (children inherit it) and the backend — so each environment keeps its own state file and its own blast radius. The parameter-group fix becomes one edit in one place, and 'prod is behind' turns into a visible source-ref bump plus a plan instead of a forgotten paste
explanation: Two different axes are being confused, and separating them is the lesson. Code duplication is solved by a module: variables are the knobs a caller turns, outputs are the results it reads back, and together they form an interface that lets the internals change without every caller being edited. Environment isolation is solved by state layout: one root per environment, each with its own backend key, so a plan in dev can only ever propose changes to dev's resources and a promotion is a deliberate act. The proposal in the prompt collapses the second axis to fix the first, which is the expensive trade: one state file and one apply mean a dev-scoped change now plans against production, an upgraded provider or a mistaken edit can propose destroying prod in the same run, and there is no way to promote a change through environments — 'in step by construction' is the loss, not the benefit, since staging exists precisely to be different from prod for a while. Indexing environments by count adds a second hazard: the instances are positional, so removing an entry shifts every later index and Terraform plans to destroy and recreate real infrastructure. Sharing one file across the three directories does deduplicate the text, but it deduplicates without an interface — there is no declared set of inputs, so per-environment differences have to be smuggled back in, and nothing signals which environments a change reaches; a module block plus variables is the mechanism designed for this, and a versioned source ref additionally lets environments adopt a change at different times. Workspaces are a genuine feature, but they solve state layout, not duplication — the 40 copy-pasted lines stay copy-pasted or become conditionals on terraform.workspace — and they weaken the very isolation that matters here: all workspaces share one backend and one configuration, so an apply against the wrong selected workspace is a live production incident with no diff in the code to review. Separate roots plus a shared module keep both axes solved at once.
